CS 301 · Meeting 12 · Recap 1

What Big O Counts

Operation counts, growth rates, and timing estimates, using the pre-class notebook and your measurements.

One line, three ways

S   = X @ W.T + b                                                 # NumPy, in the CPU's memory
S_t = X_t @ W_t.T + b_t                                           # PyTorch, on the CPU
X_d, W_d, b_d = X_t.to("cuda"), W_t.to("cuda"), b_t.to("cuda")    # every operand into the GPU's memory
S_d = X_d @ W_d.T + b_d                                           # on the GPU; S_d.cpu() brings it back
  • X (n, m), W (K, m), b (K,): the scores S have shape (n, K)
  • All tensors in an operation must use the same device
Notes. Meeting 11 used X @ W.T + b to compute a layer's scores. A neuron converts an input point into a score; a layer contains several neurons reading the same point, with their weights stored as rows of W. PyTorch uses float32 tensors here. Copy the tensors to GPU memory with .to('cuda'); .cpu() copies them back. Part 1 of the notebook asked students to write and check these steps. The figure shows group 7's image, with each pixel colored by the neuron that gives it the largest score. We now estimate the cost of this computation.

Count the operations

n×K×m
     n    m    K   passes, n x K x m   seconds   ratio to the first   nanoseconds per pass
   400   30   20             240,000     0.086                  1.0                    358
   800   30   20             480,000     0.172                  2.0                    358
   800   60   40           1,920,000     0.661                  7.7                    344
  • ×2 when n doubles; ×8 when n, m and K all double
  • Iterations: nKm, summarized as O(nKm)
  • n = m = K = size: doubling size gives ×8 iterations
Notes. The innermost statement, total += W[j, c] * X[i, c], performs one multiplication and one addition for each point, neuron, and coordinate. Compare the measured time per iteration across the three rows; processor state can affect it. O(nKm) is an asymptotic upper bound on iteration-count growth. The exact count here is nKm. Timing scales with that count only while throughput stays approximately constant. When n = m = K, the count grows as the cube of the size. Most meeting 11 posts reported a timing factor of 6 to 12 from size 2,048 to 4,096, with two reports of 2.6 and 27. The notebook now asks students to check the factor against their own table.

The count of every operation of this unit

operationin NumPycountO( )every size ×2
one neuron, one pointw @ x + b2mO(m)×2
one neuron, n pointsX @ w + b2nmO(nm)×4
a layer of K neurons, n pointsX @ W.T + b2nKmO(nKm)×8

a transpose, a reshape that returns a viewW.T, X.reshape(...)metadata onlyO(1)×1
  • O( ): how the count grows; the constant in front is dropped
  • A transpose creates a view without copying: later access costs depend on the operation (Recap 2)
Notes. The page What matrix operations cost gives these counts. When every dimension doubles, one neuron on one point takes twice as many operations, one neuron on n points takes four times as many, and a layer takes eight times as many. Elementwise functions and array addition take O(nK). A transpose changes the array metadata without copying its values: the strides are swapped, no number moves, O(1) at any size. The cost, if any, is paid by whatever consumes the view. For contiguous row- or column-major operands, X @ W.T can pass a transpose flag to BLAS and pack blocks internally; X + X.T or X.T.copy() must read one operand against the stored order, and Recap 2 measures what that costs. A reshape is also O(1) when it can return a view. These operation counts apply across machines.

The cube is not an exponential

size3: ×8 when the size doubles2size: ×2 when the size grows by one
size5121,0242,0484,096
size³134 million1.07 billion8.6 billion68.7 billion
2size155 digits309 digits617 digits1,234 digits
  • Power-law growth gives straight lines on log-log axes
  • An exponential bends upward on the same axes
Notes. One post described the measured growth as 'exponential'. Cubic growth multiplies the operation count by 8 when the size doubles. For 2 to the power size, increasing the size by one doubles the count; 2 to the power 512 already has 155 digits. On log-log axes, as in the groups' charts, a power law is a straight line and an exponential curves upward.

Your posts: the product at size 4,096

  • The same count on every machine: 137 billion operations
  • The T4: 0.049 s in 11 of 12 posts; Colab's CPU: 1.1 to 1.9 s, one at 4.0
  • GPU speedup: 22–40×, one result at 63×; median 33×
Notes. Twelve meeting 11 posts included T4 measurements. All used the same operation count. Eleven reported GPU times of 0.0486 to 0.0490 seconds. One reported 0.063 seconds and a CPU time of 3.97 seconds, roughly twice the other two-core CPU times. Colab machines are shared, and timings vary between sessions. The session with an eight-core CPU took 0.34 seconds on the CPU, giving a GPU speedup of about 7. The three posts without a GPU reported CPU times of 1.9 to 2.4 seconds. One post quoted 'typical results' of 100 to 200 times from another source; those values were excluded from the class measurements.

  • 2,048 → 4,096: ×7.5 on the CPU, ×7.2 on the T4: the count's ×8 on both
  • Similar growth rates; the T4 is about 34 times faster
Notes. One group posted its complete table. The CPU and T4 lines are nearly parallel on the log-log plot. From 2,048 to 4,096, their times increase by factors of 7.5 and 7.2, close to the factor of 8 predicted by the operation count. The T4 is about 34 times faster over these larger sizes. Big O describes the growth rate but omits this constant factor. At size 512, the T4 takes 0.17 milliseconds, and doubling to 1,024 increases its time by only 5.7. A small product uses the GPU less efficiently.

Measured operations per second

  • Measured rates range from millions to trillions of operations/second
  • Blue: measured for these slides (32 logical processors). Orange: your posts on Colab
Notes. Each row counts additions and multiplications per second. The first four rows were measured on the laptop used to build these slides, which has 32 logical processors. The last two use the class's median Colab measurements for a size-4,096 product: 1.62 seconds on a two-core CPU and 0.0487 seconds on the T4. These give about 85 billion and 2.8 trillion operations per second. The wide range of measured rates shows why operation counts alone cannot predict running time.

In Part 6, each student chose a layer, predicted its running time on both processors, and measured it. Ask two students how close their estimates were and whether layers with few neurons differed from the square-product prediction, and why.

What O( ) leaves out

time≈count×seconds for one operation
  • Operation count: O( ) describes its growth
  • Time per operation: varies with the implementation and hardware
  • Relevant factors: interpreter overhead, access order, memory, and processor
Notes. Big O describes how the operation count grows. Estimating running time also requires the time per operation, which depends on interpreter overhead, memory access order, data location, and the processor. Recap 2 compares these factors using the notebook measurements.
